questions.title: @Transactional Internals — Proxy and Propagation
questions.question: How does @Transactional work internally in Spring, and what are the main propagation levels?
questions.direct_answer: @Transactional is implemented via Spring AOP proxy. When a @Transactional method is called through the proxy, Spring opens a transaction before the method and commits or rolls back after. The behaviour across nested calls is controlled by propagation levels such as REQUIRED, REQUIRES_NEW, and NESTED.

interviewer_intent.testing: Deep understanding of Spring AOP and transaction management — not just how to annotate but what happens at runtime.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling a @Transactional method from within the same class bypasses the proxy and the transaction is silently skipped. Candidates often do not mention this self-invocation pitfall.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the self-invocation pitfall, transaction synchronisation, and how readOnly=true is a hint to the database driver to optimise for read workloads.

sections.title: @Transactional Works Through Proxies — Which Is Why Calling It From the Same Class Does Nothing
sections.content:
The most common `@Transactional` bug is self-invocation. A method in a service class calls another `@Transactional` method in the same class, expecting a transaction to start. **Nothing happens.** The transaction annotation is silently ignored because `@Transactional` works through **CGLIB proxies** — Spring creates a subclass that wraps the transactional method with `begin`, `commit`, and `rollback` logic. When you call a method on `this`, you bypass the proxy entirely.

Understanding the proxy mechanism explains every `@Transactional` gotcha: why it only works on public methods (the proxy can't override private/final methods), why self-invocation skips the transaction, and why the annotation on an interface method may not be inherited.

Beyond the proxy, the **propagation level** determines what happens when one transactional method calls another. `REQUIRED` (the default) joins the existing transaction. `REQUIRES_NEW` suspends it and creates a new one. Getting propagation wrong either silently shares transactions that should be independent or creates unnecessary transaction overhead.

sections.title: Proxy Interception — What Spring Actually Does When You Call a @Transactional Method
sections.content:
When Spring encounters a `@Transactional` bean, it creates a CGLIB proxy subclass at startup. The proxy overrides each transactional method with logic that starts a transaction before the method body and commits or rolls back after.

The call chain is: **caller → proxy → actual method → proxy (commit/rollback).** If the caller is a different bean, the call goes through the proxy. If the caller is the same class (`this.method()`), the proxy is bypassed — the call goes directly to the actual method, and Spring never sees the `@Transactional` annotation.

The fix for self-invocation is either extracting the method to a separate bean (cleanest), injecting the proxy into itself (`@Autowired private MyService self;`), or using `AopContext.currentProxy()` (least clean). In practice, extracting to a separate service is always the right answer — self-invocation usually signals that the class has too many responsibilities.

sections.title: Propagation Levels — REQUIRED, REQUIRES_NEW, and the Ones That Actually Matter
sections.content:
`REQUIRED` (the default) joins the calling transaction if one exists, or creates a new one if not. This is correct for 95% of use cases. **The subtlety: if the inner method throws a runtime exception, the outer transaction is marked for rollback** even if the outer method catches the exception. The transaction is poisoned.

`REQUIRES_NEW` suspends the current transaction and creates a completely independent one. The inner transaction can commit even if the outer rolls back. Use this for **audit logging** — you want the audit entry to persist even if the business operation fails.

`MANDATORY` requires an existing transaction and throws if none exists. Use this on methods that should never be called without a transaction — it catches bugs at development time.

**`readOnly = true`** is not a propagation level but a critical hint. It tells the JDBC driver and Hibernate to optimize for read-only access. Hibernate skips dirty checking for entities loaded in a read-only transaction, which matters when loading thousands of entities for reporting.

sections.title: The Self-Invocation Problem — Why Your @Transactional Method Is Running Without a Transaction
sections.content:
`@Transactional` works through a CGLIB proxy that wraps the bean. External callers get the proxy — the transaction starts. **But when a method calls another method within the same class**, the call goes directly to `this`, bypassing the proxy entirely. The called method runs without a transaction, even if it's annotated with `@Transactional`.

This is the most common `@Transactional` bug, and it's silent: no error, no exception, the code runs — but without transaction semantics. Changes made in the inner method aren't rolled back if an exception occurs. Writes happen immediately, not at commit time.

Three solutions, in order of preference:

**Move the method to another bean.** If `PaymentService.processPayment()` calls `this.recordAuditLog()` which needs its own transaction (`REQUIRES_NEW`), move `recordAuditLog` to `AuditLogService`. External call → proxy → transaction.

**Self-inject the proxy.** `@Autowired PaymentService self; self.recordAuditLog()` — Spring injects the proxy, so the call goes through the proxy. This is a code smell but functional for small refactors.

**`AopContext.currentProxy()`** retrieves the current proxy: `((PaymentService)AopContext.currentProxy()).recordAuditLog()`. Requires `@EnableAspectJAutoProxy(exposeProxy = true)`. Functional but ugly — prefer extracting to a new bean.

For testing: `@SpringBootTest` loads the full application context with proxies — `@Transactional` works correctly. `@ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class)` with manually wired beans bypasses proxies — `@Transactional` is ignored. This asymmetry explains why unit tests pass but integration tests reveal transaction issues.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Transactional` works through a proxy — self-invocation bypasses it** — calling `this.processOrder()` from within the same class goes through `this`, not the proxy; the transaction annotation is ignored.
- **`REQUIRED` (default) joins an existing transaction** — if a transaction is active, the method joins it; on rollback, the entire transaction rolls back, not just this method's work.
- **`REQUIRES_NEW` suspends the outer transaction and opens a new one** — the inner transaction commits or rolls back independently; costly because it requires a new database connection from the pool.
- **`NESTED` uses a savepoint inside the outer transaction** — the inner transaction can roll back to the savepoint without rolling back the outer; requires database savepoint support (not all drivers support this).
- **Default rollback is on `RuntimeException` only** — checked exceptions do not trigger rollback; use `@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)` to rollback on checked exceptions too.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@Transactional` is one of Spring's most powerful annotations — and the most misunderstood. Understanding propagation tells you exactly what happens when transactional methods call each other.

**The proxy mechanism**
- Spring wraps the bean in a proxy; when an external caller calls the annotated method, the proxy begins a transaction, calls the real method, then commits or rolls back
- `this.method()` bypasses the proxy — the call goes directly to the concrete class; no transaction is started
- Fix: inject the bean into itself, or move the called method to a separate `@Service` class

**Propagation types**
- `REQUIRED` — join existing or create new; most operations use this; rollback on the inner method rolls back everything
- `REQUIRES_NEW` — always creates a new transaction, suspending the outer; use for audit logging that must succeed even if the outer transaction rolls back; costs a second database connection
- `NESTED` — savepoint inside the outer transaction; inner rollback returns to the savepoint; outer transaction continues; requires database savepoint support
- `SUPPORTS` — joins if present, no transaction if not; use for read operations that can run either way

**Rollback rules**
- `RuntimeException` (unchecked) → rollback by default
- `Exception` (checked) → no rollback by default; add `@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)` explicitly

questions.title: Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking in JPA
questions.question: What is the difference between optimistic and pessimistic locking in JPA, and when should you use each?
questions.direct_answer: Optimistic locking uses a version column to detect concurrent updates at commit time — it fails fast without holding DB locks. Pessimistic locking acquires a DB-level lock (SELECT FOR UPDATE) to prevent concurrent access. Use optimistic for low-contention reads with occasional writes; pessimistic for high-contention or critical sections where conflicts must be prevented.

interviewer_intent.testing: Concurrency awareness — the candidate should understand both strategies, their DB-level implications, and how to implement each in JPA.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating optimistic locking as pessimistic or not knowing that OptimisticLockException must be caught and the operation retried at the application layer.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss @Version type choices (int, long, Instant), @Retryable from Spring Retry for automatic retry, and how pessimistic locking affects connection pool sizing.

sections.title: Optimistic Locking Doesn't Lock Anything — It Detects Conflicts After the Fact
sections.content:
The names are misleading. **Optimistic locking never acquires a database lock.** It adds a `@Version` column to the entity and checks it at UPDATE time: `UPDATE order SET status = 'SHIPPED', version = 3 WHERE id = 1 AND version = 2`. If another transaction already changed the row (version is now 3), the WHERE clause matches zero rows, and Hibernate throws `OptimisticLockException`. **Your application must catch this and retry** — JPA doesn't retry for you.

**Pessimistic locking acquires a real database lock** with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. No other transaction can modify the row until the lock is released at commit. This guarantees no conflicts but **holds the lock for the entire transaction duration**, blocking other transactions and potentially causing deadlocks.

The choice depends on conflict frequency. Optimistic locking works when conflicts are rare — most updates succeed, and the occasional retry is acceptable. Pessimistic locking works when conflicts are frequent and retries would cascade into more conflicts.

sections.title: Optimistic vs Pessimistic — Conflict Handling, Performance, and Connection Impact
sections.content:
The trade-off is between conflict prevention (pessimistic) and conflict detection (optimistic).

| Aspect | Optimistic | Pessimistic |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanism** | `@Version` column, check at UPDATE time | `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` database lock |
| **Lock held** | None | For entire transaction duration |
| **On conflict** | `OptimisticLockException` — app must retry | Blocks until lock released |
| **Deadlock risk** | None | Yes — two transactions locking rows in different order |
| **Throughput** | High — no blocking | Lower — serializes access |
| **Connection pool impact** | Minimal | Significant — connections held longer |
| **Best for** | Low contention, read-heavy | High contention, short critical sections |

**Connection pool impact is the hidden cost of pessimistic locking.** A locked row holds a database connection for the entire transaction. If many transactions lock rows simultaneously, the connection pool (default HikariCP `maximumPoolSize = 10`) exhausts quickly, and new requests queue or timeout. Size your connection pool based on expected concurrent locked transactions.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Optimistic locking: `@Version` column detects conflicts at commit time** — Hibernate adds `WHERE version = ?` to every UPDATE; if another transaction committed first, `OptimisticLockException` is thrown.
- **Pessimistic locking: database-level lock held for the transaction duration** — `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` (exclusive) or `SELECT ... FOR SHARE` (shared); prevents concurrent reads/writes but blocks other transactions.
- **Optimistic locking suits low-contention, read-heavy workloads** — no blocking; conflicts are rare and handled at commit; pessimistic locking suits high-contention scenarios where conflicts are frequent.
- **`@Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)` on a Spring Data method generates `SELECT FOR UPDATE`** — the row is locked until the transaction ends; other transactions block on that row.
- **`OptimisticLockException` requires a retry loop — Spring Retry helps** — wrap the operation in `@Retryable(OptimisticLockException.class)` with a max attempt count; exponential backoff prevents retry storms.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Concurrency control prevents two transactions from corrupting the same data. Optimistic and pessimistic locking are two strategies with opposite performance trade-offs.

**Optimistic locking**
- Add a `@Version` field to the entity: `@Version private Long version;`
- Hibernate includes `WHERE id = ? AND version = ?` in every UPDATE; the version column increments on each write
- If another transaction committed a change in the meantime, the `version` no longer matches; Hibernate throws `OptimisticLockException`
- No database lock held — reads are non-blocking; conflicts surface only at commit time
- Best for: user edits to records where conflicts are rare; e-commerce inventory updates with low contention

**Pessimistic locking**
- `@Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)` on the repository method → `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`
- Other transactions that try to read or write the locked row block until the lock is released at commit
- Best for: high-contention scenarios (seat reservation, bank transfer) where concurrent modifications are expected and must be serialized

**Handling `OptimisticLockException`**
- The operation must be retried with a fresh read of the entity
- `@Retryable(value = OptimisticLockException.class, maxAttempts = 3, backoff = @Backoff(delay = 100))` wraps the method automatically
- Always limit max attempts and add jitter to backoff — unlimited retries under high contention create retry storms
